about.title: About Investment Calculator
about.description: The Investment Calculator is a powerful financial planning tool that helps you project the future value of your investments based on various parameters including initial investment, regular contributions, time horizon, and expected returns. This calculator uses compound interest calculations to show how your money can grow over time. Whether you're planning for retirement, saving for a major purchase, or building wealth for the future, this calculator provides valuable insights into investment growth potential and helps you understand how different variables affect your investment outcomes.

howTo.title: How to Use the Investment Calculator

steps.title: Initial Investment
steps.description: Enter your initial investment amount (starting capital) that you plan to invest upfront.

steps.title: Monthly Contributions
steps.description: Set your monthly contribution amount if you plan to make regular additional investments.

steps.title: Time Period
steps.description: Specify the investment time period in years for your investment horizon.

steps.title: Expected Returns
steps.description: Input your expected annual rate of return based on your investment strategy and risk tolerance.

steps.title: Compound Frequency

steps.title: Review Results
steps.description: Analyze the projected investment growth, total returns, and compound interest effects.

faq.q: What's a realistic rate of return for investments?
faq.a: Historical stock market returns average around 10% annually over long periods, but conservative estimates of 6-8% are often used for planning. Bond returns are typically lower at 3-5%. Diversified portfolios might expect 7-9% long-term returns.

Most investment accounts compound daily or monthly. For planning purposes, monthly compounding is commonly used. More frequent compounding results in slightly higher returns due to the compound effect.

faq.q: Should I consider inflation in my calculations?
faq.a: Yes, inflation typically runs 2-3% annually, which reduces your purchasing power. Consider using real (inflation-adjusted) returns for more accurate long-term planning. A 7% nominal return with 3% inflation equals a 4% real return.

faq.q: What's better: lump sum or regular contributions?
faq.a: Both strategies have benefits. Lump sum investing can benefit from more time in the market, while dollar-cost averaging through regular contributions can reduce timing risk and make investing more manageable for most people.
